Your question touches on a classic pedagogical dilemma—whether to let ambiguity linger as a catalyst for inquiry, or to shepherd students toward firmer conclusions for the sake of clarity and confidence. There’s real value in both approaches, and the choice often depends on your aims for the discussion and the needs of your students.

Allowing archival uncertainties to stand can foster intellectual humility and encourage students to grapple with the provisional nature of historical knowledge. On the other hand, guiding students toward firmer conclusions can be reassuring, helping them build analytical skills and a sense of mastery over complex material. It can prevent frustration and provide a scaffold for further inquiry, especially for those who might feel adrift in ambiguity.

Perhaps there’s room for a middle path: you might let uncertainties stand for a time, inviting students to wrestle with them, and then model how historians responsibly draw conclusions from incomplete evidence—always with an eye to the limitations and possibilities of the archive. This way, you nurture both curiosity and rigor.
